title: A Booking App Cannot Fix Every Delay
description: Test whether conclusions follow from the evidence and identify assumptions that must be true for the reasoning to work.
subject: rla
author: Chee Skool
reviewNotes: Focused Arguments practice reviewed for one-best-answer logic, evidence fidelity, close distractors, and source-faithful explanations.

questions.prompt: What assumption is necessary for Lane's claim that reservations will make waiting disappear?

options.text: Customers prefer restaurants to repair shops.
options.whyWrong: Lane uses restaurants as an analogy, but his conclusion does not require this preference.

options.text: The app will be inexpensive to build.
options.whyWrong: Cost does not determine whether reservations eliminate waiting.

options.text: Scheduling is the main cause of waiting, or other major causes will somehow be removed as well.
Every customer owns a smartphone.
options.whyWrong: Access could affect use, but Lane's causal claim about eliminating waiting rests more directly on what causes delays.

explanation.whyCorrect: If major delays come from long repairs or missing parts, scheduling alone cannot logically eliminate waiting.
explanation.quickTip: For an assumption, ask: what must be true for the conclusion to follow from the reason given?

questions.prompt: Which evidence most directly challenges Lane's reasoning?

options.text: Most recorded delays were associated with long repairs or late parts rather than unscheduled arrivals.
Customers often complain about waiting.
options.whyWrong: Both managers accept that waiting is a problem; this does not challenge Lane's proposed cause.

options.text: The company operates repair shops rather than restaurants.
options.whyWrong: The important issue is whether the processes have comparable timing, not merely the industry label.

options.text: The app can send updates.
options.whyWrong: This supports one limited benefit and does not challenge the guarantee claim as directly as the delay data do.

explanation.whyCorrect: The records show that the majority of delays arise from causes an appointment system cannot remove.
explanation.quickTip: Test reasoning by looking for evidence that breaks the link between the proposed cause and the promised result.

questions.prompt: What is the main flaw in Lane's restaurant comparison?

options.text: Restaurants never use reservations.
options.whyWrong: The analogy starts from a real practice; the problem is not that reservations do not exist.

options.text: Repair duration varies with the problem being fixed, so a reservation does not control service time in the same way that a seating schedule can often control restaurant arrivals.
Repair customers are less patient than restaurant customers.
options.whyWrong: The passage gives no evidence comparing patience.

options.text: Restaurants do not need replacement parts.
options.whyWrong: Restaurants have their own supply issues; the deeper flaw is that the timing processes are not sufficiently comparable for the guarantee Lane draws.

explanation.whyCorrect: The analogy treats two scheduling situations as equivalent even though repair jobs have much more variable service duration.
explanation.quickTip: A good analogy requires the compared situations to be alike in the feature that matters to the conclusion.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion follows most reasonably from the service records?

options.text: An appointment app would have no value because it cannot fix late parts.
options.whyWrong: A tool can help with some causes without solving every cause.

options.text: The company should stop scheduling appointments entirely.
options.whyWrong: The data do not support abandoning scheduling.

options.text: Every long repair could be predicted if technicians worked faster.
options.whyWrong: The passage gives no evidence for this claim.

options.text: Scheduling improvements may address part of the waiting problem, but other operational causes must also be managed.

explanation.whyCorrect: This conclusion matches the distribution of delay causes and avoids treating one solution as either perfect or useless.
explanation.quickTip: Valid reasoning can support a limited benefit even when a proposed solution is incomplete.

questions.prompt: Which hidden assumption is most clearly exposed by Benton's response to the five-minute guarantee?

options.text: Repair shops can predict the length of each job closely enough to keep every appointment within the promised window.
Customers dislike receiving delay notifications.
options.whyWrong: Benton actually recommends faster notifications as a benefit.

options.text: All late parts are caused by customers.
options.whyWrong: The passage does not assign that cause.

options.text: The company has too few technicians.
options.whyWrong: Staffing levels are not given as a cause in the records.

explanation.whyCorrect: A five-minute guarantee only works if earlier jobs can be scheduled with enough precision to prevent them from spilling into later appointments.
explanation.quickTip: Guarantees often hide assumptions about control: ask what variable must behave predictably for the promise to hold.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes Benton's reasoning?

options.text: Because the app cannot solve every delay, the company should reject it.
options.whyWrong: Benton supports testing the app for narrower benefits.

options.text: Because customers complain, any scheduling technology will improve service.
options.whyWrong: Complaints establish a problem but do not prove a particular solution works.

options.text: The app may help with scheduling-related delays and communication, but its claims should be limited because major delay causes lie outside its control.
The company should copy restaurants because all service businesses operate the same way.
options.whyWrong: This is closer to Lane's reasoning, which Benton challenges.

explanation.whyCorrect: Benton connects the app's likely benefits to the subset of delay causes it can actually affect.
explanation.quickTip: Strong reasoning matches a solution to the problem mechanisms the evidence identifies.

questions.prompt: Which new evidence would MOST strengthen Lane's claim that exact reservations can nearly eliminate waiting?

options.text: A customer survey showing people like choosing appointment times.
options.whyWrong: Preference for scheduling does not show whether waits disappear.

options.text: A pilot showing that after the app launched, long-repair and parts delays were also controlled well enough that almost all scheduled jobs began within five minutes, across several months.
A restaurant manager explaining how table reservations work.
options.whyWrong: More information about restaurants does not show repair operations can achieve the same timing.

options.text: A screenshot of the app's appointment calendar.
options.whyWrong: The interface can show functionality but not whether real waits nearly disappear.

explanation.whyCorrect: This evidence would directly test the guarantee while addressing the operational causes that currently break Lane's assumption.
explanation.quickTip: To strengthen a claim, test the assumption that currently makes the reasoning fail.

questions.prompt: Which assumption is Lane making when he says that waiting will disappear?

options.text: A scheduling solution will somehow remove or neutralize the other major causes of delay documented in the records.
Customers dislike waiting more than technicians do.
options.whyWrong: Customer dislike of waiting does not have to be true for Lane's prediction to depend on scheduling controlling the other delay causes.

options.text: Restaurants use reservations.
options.whyWrong: The restaurant comparison is stated in the passage; the hidden assumption is that the repair shop's other delay causes will not prevent the predicted result.

options.text: The appointment app will be inexpensive to build.
options.whyWrong: Development cost could affect whether the app is worth buying, but it is not required for Lane's claim that waiting will disappear.

explanation.whyCorrect: Lane moves from a tool that mainly changes scheduling to an absolute result. That prediction requires the other documented delay causes to disappear, be controlled, or stop affecting start times.
explanation.quickTip: For an assumption question, ask what must be true for the evidence-to-conclusion jump to work.
explanation.evidenceRef: The service records show major delays from long repairs and late parts, while Lane still predicts that waiting will disappear.

curriculum.learningObjective: Test whether conclusions follow from the evidence and identify assumptions that must be true for the reasoning to work.
